currentVersionContext:
+Astrophysics and cosmology have, over the past decade, increasingly turned to machine learning to extract information from observational data---complementing rather than replacing the simulation-based inference framework introduced in Section~\ref{sec:3.2}.
+Across these fields, the way machine learning is brought to bear on the data tends to fall into two broad families, distinguished by the level at which the observables enter the model.
+The first family operates on \emph{field-level data}: the observable is treated as a spatial (or spatio-spectral) field, most commonly an image produced by a telescope or a sky map of photon counts, and a neural network is applied directly to that field.
+The second family operates on \emph{summary statistics}: each object, region, or epoch is first reduced to a low-dimensional set of features---an energy spectrum, a set of variability indicators, a handful of moments---and machine learning is applied to those features rather than to the raw signal.
+The two are not mutually exclusive, and the same scientific question can often be addressed from either angle; the choice is dictated by what the data look like, what information is preserved or discarded by a given summary, and what computational and statistical resources are available.
+The two analyses presented in this thesis fall on opposite sides of this divide and illustrate it concretely: Chapter~\ref{ch:6} works at the field level, feeding gamma-ray sky maps into a convolutional network to reconstruct the source-count distribution, while Chapter~\ref{ch:5} works with per-source spectral and variability summary statistics to search for a dark matter subhalo population among unassociated Fermi-LAT sources.

-The choice of cost function determines what the network learns.
-For a standard regression problem, the mean squared error $\mathcal{J} = \sum_i (y_i^\mathrm{true} - y_i^\mathrm{pred})^2$ penalises deviations between predictions and targets uniformly; for classification, the cross-entropy loss measures the divergence between predicted class probabilities and one-hot labels; and for neural density estimation, usually a variant of the Kuller-Leibler divergence or Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) is adopted. 
-All of them can be understood as special cases of the negative log-likelihood under an appropriate probabilistic model~\cite{bishop,Murphy:2022pml}.
-When the noise level varies across the output space, the variance can itself be parameterised as a network output, yielding the heteroscedastic Gaussian negative log-likelihood~\cite{heteroscedastic-error}; the formalism is presented in Section~\ref{sec:bayesian-error}, where Chapter~\ref{ch:6} puts it to use.
currentVersionContext:
+The choice of cost function determines what the network learns, and all of the losses used in this thesis are best understood as instances of maximum-likelihood estimation under an appropriate probabilistic model~\cite{bishop,Murphy:2022pml}.
+For a standard regression problem, the mean squared error $\mathcal{J} = \sum_i (y_i^\mathrm{true} - y_i^\mathrm{pred})^2$ penalises deviations between predictions and targets uniformly and coincides, up to constants, with the negative log-likelihood of the targets under a homoscedastic Gaussian noise model.
+For classification, the cross-entropy loss measures the divergence between predicted class probabilities and one-hot labels and is equivalently the negative log-likelihood of the observed labels under a categorical model.
+Density estimation is most commonly cast as minimising the forward Kullback--Leibler divergence between the data distribution and a parametric model; because the data-side entropy is independent of the model parameters, this minimisation is equivalent to maximising the log-likelihood of the data, and the two prescriptions yield identical gradients.
+For latent-variable models in which the marginal likelihood is intractable, this is replaced by the evidence lower bound (ELBO), a tractable lower bound on the log-marginal-likelihood that recovers maximum-likelihood estimation when the bound becomes tight.
+When the noise level varies across the output space, the Gaussian variance can itself be parameterised as a network output, yielding the heteroscedastic Gaussian negative log-likelihood~\cite{heteroscedastic-error}; the formalism is presented in Section~\ref{sec:bayesian-error}, where Chapter~\ref{ch:6} puts it to use.
